nameStory: The 'bimaculate' in this beetle's name means 'two-spotted' in Latin, referring to the pair of distinctive light-colored spots on its dark wing covers. 'Longhorn' beetles get their name from their impressively long antennae, which can be as long as or longer than their entire body. This particular species was first scientifically described by American entomologist Thomas Say in 1824, making it one of our earliest catalogued longhorn beetles.
description: The Bimaculate Longhorn Beetle is a small, slender beetle that belongs to the diverse longhorn beetle family. These beetles are easily recognized by their characteristically long, thread-like antennae and elongated body shape. Adults typically measure about 6-12mm long, making them quite small compared to many of their longhorn relatives. Their most distinctive feature is the pair of pale yellowish or whitish spots on their otherwise dark wing covers, giving them their 'two-spotted' name.

idTips.label: Two pale spots
idTips.description: Look for two distinct light-colored (yellowish to whitish) oval spots on the dark wing covers - one spot on each wing cover, positioned roughly in the middle

idTips.label: Long antennae
idTips.description: Antennae are thread-like and nearly as long as the body, feeling delicate if you gently touch them with a blade of grass

idTips.label: Small size
idTips.description: Body length is about the size of your pinky nail, roughly 6-12mm long, with a slender build that feels lightweight if handled

idTips.label: Dark body color
idTips.description: Overall coloration is dark brown to blackish, with a somewhat matte finish rather than shiny or metallic

idTips.label: Elongated shape
idTips.description: Body is notably slender and cylindrical, much longer than it is wide, giving it a stick-like appearance

habitat: Bimaculate Longhorn Beetles are found in wooded areas throughout New England, particularly in mixed deciduous and coniferous forests. They're often associated with dead or dying hardwood trees, especially oak, maple, and birch, where their larvae develop under the bark. Look for adults on flowers, tree trunks, or wooden structures like fences and decks during warm, sunny days.

seasonality.spring: Adults begin emerging in late spring as temperatures warm, often found on early blooming flowers like wild cherry or serviceberry where they feed on pollen and nectar.
seasonality.summer: Peak activity period when adults are most commonly seen on flowers, tree trunks, and around dead wood. This is the best time for identification as they're active and numerous.
seasonality.fall: Adult activity decreases significantly, though a few may still be found on late-season flowers. Larvae are developing inside dead wood during this time.
seasonality.winter: Adults are not active; larvae overwinter in galleries they've chewed inside dead hardwood trees and branches.

funFact: Despite being called longhorn beetles, the larvae of this species are actually tiny wood-boring grubs that create intricate tunnel networks under tree bark, and a single dead branch can house dozens of developing beetles creating a hidden apartment complex invisible from the outside.
confusionNotes: This beetle can be confused with other small, dark longhorn beetles, but the two pale spots are diagnostic - no other small longhorn in New England has this exact pattern. If you see the twin spots, you've found your beetle. Remember: 'bi' means two, 'maculate' means spotted.
contextualKnowledge: The scientific name 'bimaculatus' literally translates to 'two-spotted,' making this one of the more straightforward beetle names where the Latin description perfectly matches what you see in the field. This species belongs to a genus with only one representative in our region, making identification easier than with many beetle groups.
compareHints: Since this is the only Molorchus species in New England, compare it with other small longhorn beetles in the region. Unlike many of its longhorn relatives, the Bimaculate Longhorn is notably smaller and has the distinctive paired light spots rather than stripes, bands, or solid coloration. Most other small longhorns lack this specific two-spot pattern, making identification relatively straightforward once you know what to look for.
